A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but some data can help without being overly intrusive. Disability, first-gen status & financial aid are relevant to student support.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability builds trust with students & allows for tailored support. Significant accuracy gains are needed to trade it off, especially at lower explainability levels.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; perpetuating inequalities isn’t acceptable. A small decrease in overall identification to achieve fairness feels worthwhile.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach with options for follow-up feels most supportive. Twice a year is frequent enough to be proactive without being overwhelming.
A1.notes.Q7: With generic emails, reaching more is okay as it’s low-intensity. Personalized outreach should be targeted & avoid burdening those not needing help.
A1.Q8.1: I'm concerned about the potential for 'gaming' of the system—students altering behavior to appear less at risk, hindering genuine support efforts.

A2.notes.Q3: Privacy is key, but some data improves identification of struggling students. Sensitive info needs a *very* strong justification. Focusing on equity through adjustments is important.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for trust with students and advisors. We need to understand *why* a student is flagged, even if it reduces accuracy slightly. Beyond a certain point, black box models aren't acceptable.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness can’t be sacrificed for overall performance. A small reduction in total identification is acceptable if it means closing gaps and avoiding biased outcomes. We *must* prioritize equity.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is more effective. Offering a meeting provides direct support, but an email is less intrusive as the first step. Twice yearly checks seem reasonable.
A2.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach requires careful targeting. We shouldn't bombard students, but a slightly higher threshold for personalized contact is okay as it’s more valuable.
A2.Q8.1: The survey largely focused on data and algorithmic fairness. I also worry about the resources needed to *respond* effectively to flagged students – adequate staffing for support services is essential.

A3.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but some data can help identify vulnerable students. Sensitive categories need strong justification for inclusion and must prioritize fairness.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust with students and advisors. Tradeoffs are acceptable if there's moderate accuracy gain, but low/very low explainability aren’t viable.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital. Some decrease in overall identification is acceptable to ensure equitable support across all student groups – we don't want to widen existing gaps.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is more impactful, but offers a student choice to meet. Twice-yearly feels like a good balance – frequent enough without being overwhelming.
A3.notes.Q7: With generic email, slightly fewer targeted contacts seem fair. Personalised interventions need more care and require better targeting to not cause stress/wasted effort.
A3.Q8.1: The survey doesn't address the resources available to respond to increased demand if this model identifies more students needing support. That needs planning.

S1.notes.Q3: It's a slippery slope with personal data. Focusing on performance seems safer, but financial situation *can* impact study success, so some consideration is okay if it improves fairness.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially knowing my own history with dropping out. A lack of transparency feels controlling. Less accuracy is fine if I understand *why*.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness matters a lot, given that some groups already face barriers. Missing a few students overall is better than reinforcing existing inequalities.
S1.notes.Q6: A simple email seems least intrusive, but a personalized one might be more effective. Constant contact would feel overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: For general info, missing some is okay. But personalized advice requires more care – you don't want to bother people who are doing fine.
S1.Q8.1: I worry about the 'creep' of surveillance and how this system could be used beyond just offering support. Clear boundaries are essential.

S2.notes.Q3: Data privacy is paramount. Adding data beyond credits & performance feels invasive, especially Absalon activity. Financial aid might be relevant but requires careful consideration.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially for students from different educational backgrounds like myself. Less explainability feels untrustworthy.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial; it’s not acceptable to worsen outcomes for any group. A small decrease in overall accuracy is okay if it means equal opportunity.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels more supportive than generic emails. An invitation to talk provides a real chance for help, but not constantly.
S2.notes.Q7: With general information, contacting more students is less harmful. But personalized outreach needs to be targeted; false positives are intrusive.
S2.Q8.1: The survey focuses a lot on data and accuracy, but doesn’t really address the underlying reasons *why* students struggle - financial stress, cultural adjustment etc. Addressing these root causes is just as important!

S3.notes.Q3: I’m very cautious about privacy, especially with sensitive data. Disability *could* be helpful for targeted support, but only if it actively improves fairness and doesn't just reinforce bias.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for building trust, but it shouldn’t come at a huge cost to accuracy. A little less explainability is okay if it significantly helps more students.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness matters massively, especially given my own experiences navigating the system with a disability. It’s unacceptable to exacerbate existing inequalities. A slight dip in overall identification is worth it.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized contact feels less intrusive and more supportive, but offering a meeting gives students space to proactively engage if they want to. Twice a year is frequent enough for timely support without being overwhelming.
S3.notes.Q7: With generic email, it's better to err on the side of caution and not overwhelm people. But with a personalized approach from an advisor, striking a balance feels right.
S3.Q8.1: I worry about students self-censoring their struggles if they fear being flagged by this system – especially those already hesitant to seek help. It needs to be *very* clear this isn't punitive.

S4.notes.Q3: Privacy is really important, especially given my past dropout. But disability info *could* help identify issues if used to improve fairness. It’s a fine line.
S4.notes.Q4: The more opaque it is, the less trust there will be – and that’s a big problem for actually getting help. Some loss of accuracy to get clarity is okay.
S4.notes.Q5: Equal outcomes are vital; otherwise, this just reinforces existing inequalities. A small dip in overall identification is worth it if it means more equitable support.
S4.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and more helpful than generic blasts. But continuous monitoring is too much.
S4.notes.Q7: Fewer personalized interventions are better than lots of unnecessary ones, especially given my own experiences with being overwhelmed.
S4.Q8.1: It’s important the system doesn't assume *why* someone is struggling. My ADHD significantly impacts my studies but looks different to what the model might expect.

S5.notes.Q3: Privacy feels crucial, especially as an international student new to the system. Adding Absalon data is a hard no. Nationality *could* be useful for targeted support programs but only if it demonstrably improves fairness.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is very important for trust. A model needs to be understandable enough to feel like help, not surveillance. I'd trade some accuracy for that.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable. If it systematically disadvantages any group, the system isn’t acceptable. A small decrease in overall identification to achieve this is worthwhile.
S5.notes.Q6: Personalized support is key, but needs to be voluntary. Twice a year feels like enough outreach without being overwhelming. I'd want the option of just receiving an email and declining further contact.
S5.notes.Q7: For generic emails, I think reaching more students is okay even with some false positives. But personalized outreach should be more targeted to avoid wasting resources or making people uncomfortable.
S5.Q8.1: It would be helpful to know how the model's predictions are validated and regularly updated. There needs to be a way to appeal if a student feels they were incorrectly flagged.

S6.notes.Q3: I’m cautious about too much data collection, especially sensitive info. Improvement needs to be significant for it to be worth the privacy risk. Nationality and first-gen status feel particularly relevant in my experience.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially given I switched programs. Knowing *why* the model flagged me would be helpful for adjusting my approach. Lower explainability isn’t worth a small improvement in accuracy.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial! It's unacceptable if the model unfairly disadvantages certain groups, like international students who might already face more challenges. A small reduction in overall accuracy for fairness is worth it.
S6.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and might get lost. A personalized email or invitation to speak with an advisor feels more supportive, but not *too* frequent.
S6.notes.Q7: For general support info, contacting more students is okay if the impact isn’t huge. But for personalized outreach, it's better to be selective and ensure resources aren't stretched too thin.
S6.Q8.1: I worry about the model reinforcing existing biases – maybe because I switched programs once, it might unfairly flag me again. A human check is crucial before any intervention.

S7.notes.Q3: I'm wary of using too much personal data, but knowing I have dyslexia and get support already makes me feel more comfortable with that info being used to *help* rather than judge.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially with learning differences. I need to understand why something’s flagged. A black box isn't helpful – it makes me anxious.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is key. Missing students who need help because of their background is unacceptable. A slight dip in overall identification is worth it if it means everyone gets a fair shot.
S7.notes.Q6: A generic email feels impersonal. Personalized outreach or inviting me to talk it through is more helpful. Contacting too often would be annoying though.
S7.notes.Q7: Personalized contact needs to be careful. False positives are worse when they're individual, but a general 'heads up' is okay. Don’t want to overwhelm advisors.
S7.Q8.1: It would be good to know how the model handles students with diagnosed learning difficulties like myself – does it account for that in its predictions?

S8.notes.Q3: I'm very wary of data collection, especially anything beyond what is absolutely necessary for academic assessment. First-gen status and financial aid are okay with some fairness benefits.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust and so students understand why they're being contacted, but a little loss of accuracy is acceptable if it means the model is much clearer.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness *has* to be prioritized. If the system reinforces existing disadvantages, it's worse than useless. A slight decrease in overall identification is worth a more equitable approach.
S8.notes.Q6: Generic emails will likely be ignored. Personalized contact, with the option to meet someone, feels more supportive and less like automated surveillance.
S8.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach needs more care - fewer false positives are crucial. A general email can tolerate a slightly higher rate of unnecessary contact.
S8.Q8.1: The biggest concern is the potential for reinforcing existing biases, particularly for students from non-traditional backgrounds like mine. The model must be continually monitored and adjusted to address these issues.

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is key, but some data could genuinely help if used responsibly. Disability info warrants more consideration than others due to potential for bias.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust and to ensure students feel understood, not just labelled by an algorithm. A moderate trade-off seems reasonable.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness *must* be prioritised, even if it means identifying slightly fewer students. Focusing on recall is crucial for marginalized groups.
S9.notes.Q6: Personalised outreach offers more targeted support and builds trust, but isn't intrusive like a phone call. Twice yearly feels reasonable.
S9.notes.Q7: With general info, erring on the side of fewer contacts is better. Personalized outreach allows more targeted support so balance is preferable.
S9.Q8.1: The model should be transparent about its limitations and not presented as a definitive judgement. Also, the potential for creating self-fulfilling prophecies needs consideration.
